high.title: Exported service MyService has no permission protection
high.description: Service "edu.ksu.cs.benign.MyService" is reachable by any app on the device (android:exported="true") and declares no permission. MyService is exported and guarded by 'santos.benign.permission', but this custom permission is declared with a 'normal' protection level, allowing any app to request and obtain it.
high.impact: Any unprivileged app on the device can start MyService, which in turn launches the SensitiveActivity with a success status.
high.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if it is internal, or guard it with a signature-level permission and validate all input.

medium.title: Permission check reads the app's own identity, not the caller's
medium.description: enforcePermission() reads Binder.getCallingPid() in onStartCommand(), outside any binder call, so it checks this app's own permissions rather than those of whoever started the component. The permission check in MyService.onStartCommand calls enforcePermission, which is indicated to read the app's own identity instead of the caller's identity, effectively bypassing the guard.
medium.impact: The service is accessible to any app regardless of whether it holds the required permission.
medium.code_snippet: enforcePermission("santos.benign.permission", android.os.Binder.getCallingPid(), android.os.Binder.getCallingUid(), "Not allowed to start MyService");

lines: public int onStartCommand(android.content.Intent intent, int flags, int startId) {
android.util.Log.d("MyService", "Calling PID = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingPid() + " Calling UID  = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingUid());
enforcePermission("santos.benign.permission", android.os.Binder.getCallingPid(), android.os.Binder.getCallingUid(), "Not allowed to start MyService");
lines_html: public int onStartCommand(android.content.Intent intent, int flags, int startId) {
android.util.Log.d("MyService", "Calling PID = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingPid() + " Calling UID = " + android.os.Binder.getCallingUid());
enforcePermission("santos.benign.permission", android.os.Binder.getCallingPid(), android.os.Binder.getCallingUid(), "Not allowed to start MyService");
android.util.Log.d("MyService", "Service Started");
android.content.Intent activityIntent = new android.content.Intent(this, (java.lang.Class<?>) edu.ksu.cs.benign.SensitiveActivity.class);
activityIntent.addFlags(268435456);
activityIntent.putExtra("status_msg", "SUCCESS");

medium.recommendation: Guard the component with android:permission in the manifest; check a caller's permission with checkCallingPermission() only inside a binder call.

info.title: Application is debuggable in this build
info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The application is marked as debuggable in the manifest. This allows an attacker with ADB access to attach a debugger, inspect memory, and execute arbitrary code in the app's context.
info.impact: Full runtime access to the app's process and data on any device with adb.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: Missing screenshot protection
info.description: The application does not set FLAG_SECURE on its activities, allowing sensitive screen contents to be captured via screenshots or screen recordings.
info.impact: Sensitive information displayed in the app can be leaked through system-level screenshots or the recents screen.
info.recommendation: Apply FLAG_SECURE to windows displaying sensitive data.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 permits cleartext traffic by default
info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in. The app targets SDK 27, which allows cleartext HTTP traffic by default, and lacks a Network Security Configuration to restrict it.
info.impact: Sensitive data transmitted over HTTP can be intercepted via MITM attacks.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The app targets SDK 27 and uses default taskAffinity, making it vulnerable to task hijacking on Android 10 and lower.
info.impact: A malicious app can overlay its own activities on top of the app's activities by using the same task affinity.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
